utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The Defence will bring evidence to show that Goran Hadzic is neither individually responsible nor responsible as a superior for the Prosecution's allegations of crimes against humanity and war crimes committed in Croatia between 25th of June, 1991, and the end of 1993. Neither is Mr. Hadzic responsible for the permanent removal of Croat and other non-Serbs population from a large part of the territory of Republic of Croatia through the commission of crimes in violation of Articles 3 and 5 of the Statute. The Defence will present evidence that no joint criminal enterprise existed between Mr. Hadzic and individuals listed in paragraph 10 of the Prosecution's indictment. Mr. Hadzic entered into no agreement with them, and Mr. Hadzic did not possess the intent to permanently remove the non-Serb population from the territory of SBWS or the RSK. Indeed, he did not commit any crime alleged in the indictment and deserves acquittal on all counts. The Defence has already challenged the evidence of some Prosecution witnesses in its cross-examination. Your Honours will now soon hear direct evidence that they lied to the Court in the relevant parts of their testimony. The most drastic cases of dishonesty which the Defence will rebut are GH30, GH03, GH07, GH10, GH116, GH044, GH15, GH16, GH23, GH24, GH26, GH124, GH135, GH154, GH102, GH027, GH110, and GH28. We shall also prove that some documents admitted into evidence are false. From the first day of trial, in its opening statement, Prosecution attempted to present Mr. Hadzic as a violent man with the sinister plan to harm non-Serbs. As Your Honours get to know him personally in the coming weeks, Your Honours will see that he is in fact an ordinary man who loves his family. A former warehouse worker from a small village in Slavonia called Pacetin, which in 1991 had less than a thousand inhabitants. He was a man concerned about direction of his country's rapidly changing politics and who joined a local party and was propelled to his position by a series of events out of his control. And that would change his life forever. Your Honours well know about his arrest in Plitvice on 31st of March, 1991, and how those events put him in the nation's spot light in ways he could not predict. Indeed, the Defence will present evidence that Mr. Hadzic was often so out of his league, he was rarely privy to sensitive and confidential information. Even an ordinary man like Mr. Hadzic could see the writing on the wall as Yugoslavia began to crumble. Like many Serbs in Croatia, he felt frustrated, powerless, and indeed scared when he witnessed increasing violence directed at his fellow Serbs, discrimination against them in their workplaces, and harassment, and terror. The rising tensions in the early 1990s displayed in media and around the country reminded him of his grandfather, who in World War II was murdered by members of the Fascist regime. His own father was a partisan who fought in the war. His memory was like that of the memories of so many Croatian Serbs, many of which had close relatives who suffered in decades past. These were not memories easily forgotten or dismissed by people, but Mr. Hadzic had no place to escape. Everything he had was in Pacetin. His home, his land, his job, his memories. He could not accept a future where he and his family would live in fear. He took action. He would learn later, sadly, that the destiny of the Serb people in the SBWS not to remain in Yugoslavia was already sealed. At the time they still held on to hope that they could fight and sacrifice to preserve the status quo. In 1990, Mr. Hadzic joined a political party and got involved in the politics of his village. He hoped to change the system from within, legally and peacefully. The Defence will bring witnesses who, as members of government, saw first-hand that Mr. Hadzic sought political comprise through negotiations. They will discuss how he became a member of the multi-ethnic SDP party, led by Croat politician Ivica Racan, in part because their political platform sought to keep Croatia within Yugoslavia. Mr. Hadzic entered into politics for that very reason: To preserve the status quo so that he and his family would be safe. When the SDP leadership abandoned its pro-Yugoslav policy, however, Mr. Hadzic could no longer support them. He joined the SDS, the only political party that remained which adopted the platform of preserving Yugoslavia and indeed the only political party in Croatia that would protect the rights of Serbs and Croats alike. The Defence will prove that Mr. Hadzic did his best to avoid the war and to maintain a working and functional relationship with the Croatian government. Your Honours will hear evidence from Mr. Hadzic himself and other witnesses about when Mr. Hadzic met with the late president of Croatia, Franjo Tudjman, and his other communication and negotiations with members of the government of Croatia such as Josip Boljkovac and Slavko Degoricija. Your Honours will note that his efforts at communications and negotiations continued even after his arrest at Plitvice, even after he had been beaten by Croatian police in detention, even after he, of all people, may have had reason to change his approach. And yet he remained on the path of peaceful resolution. This path was only blockaded when Croatia declared its independence. Your Honours heard in the Prosecution's opening statement a one-sided understanding of the breakup of Yugoslavia. That opening statement skipped over crucial historical background and context of the events described in the indictment. Your Honours will therefore hear a number of witnesses who worked in the government ministry as well as a historian, a legal expert, and a demographer who will offer that context. In short, Your Honours, if you place yourselves in the shoes of the leaders of the former Yugoslavia in 1991, your understanding of the events would be that Croatia had seceded from the state and began an armed insurgency against the prevailing state and its army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. I repeat the last sentence. Your Honours will therefore hear a number of witnesses who worked in the government ministry as well as a historian, a legal expert, and a demographer who will offer that context. In short, Your Honours, if you place yourselves in the shoes of the leaders of the former Yugoslavia in 1991, your understanding of the events would be that Croatia had seceded from the state and began an armed insurgency against the prevailing state and its army. Importantly, the Prosecution's opening statement neglected a crucial distinction between Yugoslavia and Croatia in 1991. While in 1991 Yugoslavia was an internationally recognised state, a member of the United Nations, and otherwise a subject of international law, Croatia was just a territory in Yugoslavia. A territory's unilateral proclamation of the independence, whether based in a referendum or not, whether deriving from a decision of its Assembly on 25th of June, 1991, does not make it an independent state just like that. Of course, it could certainly be the first step towards independence but not the final one, and it certainly would not take immediate effect either locally or under international law. Indeed, as Your Honours will see in the video we will show you, analysts had predicted that Croatia's attempt to secede from Yugoslavia would likely end in violence. Yugoslavia meanwhile saw the referendum, the Assembly decision, and the events that ensued as an act of secession in contravention of her constitution. From that point of view, such an act was an attack on the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the country as a whole. The federal authorities including the JNA, the authorities of the federal units, other local authorities, and all citizens still, regardless of the upheaval, had the constitutional obligation to defend the territorial integrity of Yugoslavia. Therefore, the engagement of the JNA from the very onset of the conflict was the legitimate act of the state in protection of its territorial integrity. The Defence will demonstrate that the JNA was present in the parts of Croatia during the whole 1991 and first half of 1992 in order to carry out its duties under law and in an effort to preserve a rapidly dissolving state. By virtue of JNA's presence in the areas designated as SAO Krajina, SAO Western Slavonia, and SBWS, later known as RSK, during the armed conflict, signified that the military was in total control of the territory, its material resources, and its manpower. That authority would persist completely for all the events on the territory held by the JNA's units until its withdrawal in June 1992. The Defence will provide the Chamber with a number of military orders, judicial acts of the military courts and their security organs which will definitely prove the JNA's ongoing de facto authority in the region. Your Honours have already seen a high-ranking JNA officer, General Zivota Panic, unabashedly claiming command over the volunteer units of Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, and Vojislav Seselj. The Prosecution's case and indictment glossed over Panic's incriminating admissions and indeed avoided mention of all military men in the region who were actively commanding all units and exercising authority through 1991 and 1992. Those military men that the Chamber did hear conveniently shifted their responsibility to the local Serbs from Croatia. The Prosecution also neglected that the proclaimed independence of Croatia, whether that alone created a new independent state or not, was not just a political act. The Defence will demonstrate that as a result of the Serb population's vote which declared to remain in Yugoslavia, the Serbs were exposed to a series of organised and systematic violence in order to neutralize or at least minimise their opposition. The elimination of Serbs from the Croatian constitution in 1990s was followed with massive dismissal of the Serbs from the Croatia state administration, primarily from the police, thus depriving Serbs of the protection of the state. Serbs felt intimidated as public rallies widely promoted through media broadcast anti-Serb speeches, and symbols, emblems and songs from the independent state of Croatia which was deliberately reminiscent of the fascist regime under the patronage of Nazi Germany. Their use of these symbols reminded Serbs of the horrors that their parents and grandparents suffered during the time, simply because they were not Croatian or Catholics. Following these intimidating rallies came blasting, shooting, arson, and destruction of Serb property. Physical violence flourished, resulting in the disappearance, injuries, and killings of Serbs. It considerably reduced the presence and the political influence of Serbs in Croatia on the upcoming events. The Defence will demonstrate that by 14 July 1991 that strategy brought 11.867 refugees to Serbia. In the next six weeks, the number increased to 77.000. Contrary to evidence brought by the -- sorry. These refugees originated from Croatia because the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina had not yet begun. The most significant number of them arrived in Vukovar and the territory SBWS due to inadequate protection from violent attacks. In conditions of anarchy, violence, and chaos, only the federal authority had the power to prevent massive attacks and protect its citizens. The JNA was only federal force present in Croatia. Croatian forces therefore carried out a different attack strategy. They neutralised the JNA by encircling the commands, units, premises, and military personnel. The JNA's communication and supplies were cut off. The Croatian forces' efforts were indeed effective, as some of these units surrendered. Others resisted. These attacks were illegal, and the JNA the right and duty both to resist and fight the attackers. The Defence will offer evidence which will truly and accurately present the events described in paragraphs 24 to 38 of the indictment. Therefore, the attacks on the JNA and its subordinate units in Croatia in 1990 and 1991 was an armed insurgency on the territory of an internationally recognised state. The military of the state, including all her authorities and citizens, had both legal and legitimate right to respond to those attacks with force. That response, legitimate in the eyes of both military commanders and civilian leaders at the time, negates the Prosecution's position that the goal was to force the permanent removal of Croats and other non-Serbs. Your Honours will hear from Mr. Hadzic himself that he was not aware of any authority from the territory of the former Yugoslavia which stood behind such a policy. Your Honours will hear from the leaders of disparate factions that took advantage -- sorry. Mr. Hadzic, in his capacity as president of SBWS government and president of -- president, did not support or assist position that would intentionally target non-Serbs. In any event, crimes were happening everywhere, against anyone, regardless of ethnicity, in a way that the government could not fully control despite its best efforts. The Prosecution presumes that the instant in which a government is formed, it will immediately have all the resources, manpower, laws, and basic institutions necessary to make it legitimate, functioning, and capable of restoring peace and order. This proposition is naive and unrealistic. The supposition is similar to expecting government of Iraq to be perfectly functioning the day after Saddam Hussein was toppled. The reality was that Mr. Hadzic's newborn government lacked the most basic resources, including telephones, typewriters and paper, let alone manpower, training, and supplies. The local civilian police were hobbled in the face of total chaos, conflict, and war. Your Honours will see that, in spite of that, Mr. Hadzic's government undertook trial numerous criminal investigations, generating many police and judicial documents which were brought against Serbs for crimes committed against Croats and other non-Serbs. These documents will definitely show that Mr. Hadzic and his government endeavoured to enforce the law and punish the perpetrators of crimes, regardless of the ethnicity of the victim, as best they could, in a very, very bad situation. This evidence will directly undermine that the Prosecution's bold assertion that in the face of secession, dissolution of the state, armed conflict, and ensuing anarchy, Mr. Hadzic must have intended for neighbours to commit crimes against their neighbours as part of a broader plan. The Defence will show the Chamber a video entitled: "Yugoslavia: The Avoidable War." The video is in English with B/C/S subtitles. Unfortunately, we do not have a transcript at this time. This video contains the recollection of many international statesmen, scholars and journalists who participated and followed the events in the former Yugoslavia and Croatia and produced a recollection to the relevant events. We will play it for 47 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: "Night after night, television brought images of death and suffering from the war that engulfed Yugoslavia between 1991 and 1995. When the fighting stopped, NATO countries, particularly the United States, eagerly claimed credit for ending the war. The lesson learned, many said, was that there should be early intervention in ethnic conflicts, and preferably by NATO. But did the West prematurely take credit for ending a war it had helped create? Did misguided Western intervention actually transform a small brush fire in the Balkans into a major civil war. "I think that what the international community on the whole, the Europeans and the Americans and the United Nations have done, on the whole made it sure there was going to be a conflict. "The intelligence community was unanimous in saying that if we go ahead and recognise Bosnia, it will blow up. "Because there was no agreed branches and because everybody was armed, if you ruptured the old Yugoslavia by unilaterally declaring independence, in fact seceding, it was a war of secession, once you decided to secede, you had no hope that it could be done peacefully "Early 1990 had brought a brief moment of hope and optimism to Europe as the Berlin Wall crumbled and the Cold War ground to a halt. A new united Germany stood poised to unite the rest of Europe through its leadership of the European community, a friendly but powerful rival to the United States. But the promise of European unity was short-lived. Just two years later, much of Yugoslavia was in flames. A small war in the Slovenian Republic led to larger, more bloody conflicts in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. Moreover, European nations, the United States, and Middle Eastern states were backing different factions in these outbreaks of civil war. "Publicly, Western diplomats blamed irresponsible ethnic leaders of the different Yugoslav republics for the bloodshed, including Milan Kucan of Slovenia, Franjo Tudjman of Croatia, and especially Slobodan Milosevic in Serbia. There was certainly no innocence among the warring parties. "Privately, however, European community envoy Lord Carrington and UN mediator Cyrus Vance were furious at Germany's foreign minister, Hans-Dietrich Genscher. Vance would later call the conflict Mr. Genscher's war because of Germany's push to recognise separatists in Slovenia and Croatia. "Vance argued that recognition would take away the diplomatic leverage that he had to try to bring the conflict in Croatia to an end and could possibly result in Bosnia blowing up. "The former German foreign minister claimed that his government did not support the breakup of Yugoslavia until fighting began. "We held a strong position for the unity of Yugoslavia, as I said, but we saw that the will to keep it together vanished more and more under the pressure of military events. "In fact, however, since the 1960s, Germany's intelligence arm, the BND, was deeply involved in the training of Croatian separatists led by the pro-Nazi Ustashi who fled to Germany after World War II and participated in a number of terrorist actions against embassies and the government of Yugoslav communist leader Josip Broz Tito. "In the early 1960s, the BND decided to cooperate fully with the Ustasha. This became plain to see after the so-called Croat Spring in the beginning of the 1970s. After Tito's death, they accelerated their efforts, together with the Ustasha, in order to disintegrate Yugoslavia into several smaller states. "Germany's crucial role in supporting Croatian separatists is confirmed by Anton Duhacek, the former director of Yugoslav counterintelligence, who was himself a Croat. "The Germans wanted an absolute and complete subordination of Croatian intelligence that would carry out all that the Germans wanted, and the Germans promised that this would be in the interest of the future independent, free Croatia. "On the surface, Yugoslavia seemed better off than its East European neighbours in the 1970s and 1980s. The US considered its independent communist leader, Josip Broz Tito, an asset in the Cold War with Moscow. Yugoslavia's economy was propped up with Western loans even after Tito's death in 1980. The carefully staged 1984 Olympics in Sarajevo offered the world the impression of a peaceful multi-ethnic country working together. Veteran observers, however, could see trouble below the surface. "I think the first hint I got of violent breakup was when I made a tour of all of the republics in 1983 and I heard a lot of, sort of, separatist sentiments in several of the republics, especially Slovenia and Croatia but not only, and some very threatening remarks were made in the course of my conversations about what we would do to them and so on. "By themselves, neither Slovenia nor Croatia had the diplomatic or military power to actually separate, to challenge Yugoslavia's federal army, which was the fourth largest in Europe. But Germany provided not only diplomatic support but also weapons, even after an international arms embargo "And I wrote a story about it which was called: 'The blockade's a joke.' And so I went and started checking the ports, like Split and the ports along the Dalmatian coast, and as best I could checking the stuff that was coming across the borders and there was no limitation. "We saw a Croatian MiG-21 shot down in the Krajina which the Croatians said came from former Yugoslavia air force stocks. In fact, it was clearly from Eastern German air force stocks and had the East German radar warning receivers on board. So we know that these weapons are coming from the former East German stocks, and that they are, if you like, slightly disguised in the sense that it looked like Western German weapons. They are coming from West Germany, obviously with the West German government's blessing. There can no other way in which heavy weapons can be supplied like this. "While separatist forces were being armed, Germany was at the same time warning the Yugoslav government of Ante Markovic not to use force against separatists. Ante Markovic, who was himself a Croatian, presided over a divided government which was unable to stand up to German pressure or rally his government for the challenges ahead. "He never lined up, you know, coalition support. He always flew solo. So, you know, he could be welcomed in the White House and was but didn't have any backing at home. So in that sense he was a real failure and a disastrous one in that he preserved the fiction that Yugoslavia was holding together. "The Yugoslav federal army, which held the country together, now became a target for those who wanted to break it apart. At a Croatian separatist rally in Split in May of 1991, demonstrators strangled the young soldier of the federal army and then tossed his dead body onto the street. This and similar events seemed to bear out predictions by the US Central Intelligence Agency. "The CIA said, in 1990, October, that Yugoslavia faced breakup, probably violent, as early as six months from the time of the report and nobody paid any attention to it in the higher echelons of government. "By June of 1991, however, US Secretary of State James Baker decided to make one attempt to prevent a disaster. He flew to Belgrade, the capital of Yugoslavia, to confront leaders of six republics. "And he said, 'Don't any of you take steps that are not agreed on by the others.' "However, Milan Kucan and Franjo Tudjman, leaders of the Slovenian and Croatian republics, were confident that they could ignore the US Secretary of State. They declared their independence just days later on June 25th. Because they could count on the support of German Foreign Minister Genscher and Austrian Foreign Minister Alois Mock. "The cycle of violence which would destroy Yugoslavia began when Slovene President Milan Kucan ordered his troops to seize customs posts on Yugoslav borders with Austria and Italy and the Slovene capital of Ljubljana. Yugoslav flags were taken down and replaced with Slovenian flags. "And Slovenes thought they had a right to take down those flags, the end of an internationally recognised [indiscernible], and I don't think that the -- for a moment Belgrade expected there would be violent resistance. "To avoid violence, Yugoslav army general Andrija Raseta had phoned Milan Kucan privately to let him know that many Yugoslav army troops responding to this challenge of federal authority were not even carrying live ammunition. "But in fact, the Slovenes had prepared themselves. They were getting a lot of encouragement from across the way, from Vienna and from the Germans too, and they foresaw that they could make a very big international case by having what they called a war of independence. It was nothing of the sort. "German Foreign Minister Hans-Dietrich Genscher flew to the Austrian border with Yugoslavia to join President Kucan and warn the federal army against efforts to maintain control of federal borders. Kucan ordered his forces to fire on Yugoslav army troops, including those who carried no live ammunition. Faced with international opposition led by Germany, Yugoslav President Markovic ordered the federal army to withdraw from Slovenia without a serious attempt to counter separatist forces. "Slovene leaders conducted a masterful public relations effort. Foreign reporters were kept occupied in an underground press centre with briefings that suggested that Slovene forces had defeated the fourth largest army in Europe. Journalists in the press centre routinely reported as news fanciful briefings from Slovene officials on various battles including some that had never happened. "What was going on in Slovenia, where the Slovenians declared independence and set up customs posts on the road, tended to be seen and portrayed on television as the -- the Yugoslav army acting aggressively against Slovenia as opposed to the Slovenians declaring independence "The manipulation of the foreign press corps set the tone for new wars of secession in Croatia and Bosnia. Repeatedly, the JNA was described as an occupying force dominated by Serbs. The reality was different, however. The army's Chief of Staff, Veljko Kadijevic, was half Croatian, half Serb. Air force chief Zvonko Jurjevic was Croatian, and the commander of the navy, Stane Brovet, was Slovenian. "The federal army had held Yugoslavia together under Tito without creating any protests about human rights. Tito insisted on an ethnic balance, and in the localities it was composed of the people of that area. It was absurd to call it an army of occupation. And we should have - we the West - should have recognised that until there was an agreed arrangement for a dissolution of a state which had been Yugoslavia and which might take years or decades would perhaps be impossible. Until then, it had to be recognised these were the internationally recognised branches. "If German and Austrian leaders still believed that Slovenia and Croatia could be separated from Yugoslavia without a wider war, the Americans strongly believed otherwise. "Because we said if Yugoslavia does not break up peacefully, there's going to be one hell of a civil war. It nevertheless broke up non-peacefully. It broke up through the unilateral declaration of independence by Slovenia and Croatia and the seizing by these two countries, republics, of their border posts, which was an act of force and which was an act that was in violation of the Helsinki principles. But the European powers and the United States ultimately recognised Slovenia and then Croatia and then Bosnia as independent countries as member -- and admitted them to the United Nations. The real problem was that there was a unilateral declaration of independence and a use of force to gain that independence rather than a peaceful negotiation of independence, which is the way it should have happened. "While most of Europe, including England, France and Russia, opposed the breakup of Yugoslavia, only the Americans were strong enough to oppose Germany. In a decision that would have far-reaching consequences, however, the Americans decided to back away from this challenge. George Kenney, who would later resign in protest over policy, was running the US State Department's Yugoslavia desk at the time "Our marching orders were to keep the US out to -- to -- to avoid taking any responsible for a solution to the conflict. The analysts could see that the problem would get a lot worse. They also saw that the Europeans weren't going to be able to handle it. "Historically, the United States had supported a multi-ethnic Yugoslavia over a 70-year period, to stabilize the region and serve as a barrier to German expansion. In reality, Yugoslavia, a union of South Slavic peoples, would never have come together in 1918 without American support from US President Woodrow Wilson. "For centuries, the region had been colonised by Austro-Hungary and the Turkish Ottoman Empire. The Austrians, under the Hapsburg monarchy, used a policy of divide and rule to maintain control, keeping the Slovenes, Croatians, Serbs, and Muslims at each other's throats, instead of uniting them in their common interests "The Hapsburg Empire kept going and held down large parts of what we tend to call Yugoslavia, and there was no possibility of a Slav get-together until after the First World War when the Austro-Hungarian Empire collapsed and the peoples came together and decided to unite. "With American support, Yugoslavia was founded in 1918 and survived German attempts to divide it up during World War II. When Yugoslavia's communist leader Josip Broz Tito broke away from the Soviet Union and the Eastern Bloc in 1948, the US stepped in with military assistance as well as international loans to prop up a buffer state between the West and the communist-dominated Warsaw Pact. As the Cold War came to an end, however, Washington declared a new world order which emphasised economic competition rather than anti-Communism. "So once that containment of the Soviet Union began to disappear as a need with the decline in -- after mid-1980s, Gorbachev's economic reforms, the NATO Warsaw Pact, talks about reducing arms and force build-up, all of that led to Yugoslavia being essentially irrelevant in its defence posture. And by early 1989, the Americans were really quite explicit. The ambassador -- new ambassador to Yugoslavia from the United States informed the Yugoslav government that the Yugoslav position was no longer needed, that it was no longer -- Yugoslavia was no longer strategically important to the United States and Western defence. "Yugoslavia had become expendable. International loans were called in, causing triple-digit inflation. The federal government was forced to require austerity measure from the different republics, "Particularly those requirements led Slovenia as a republic and eventually other republics to rebel against what was being called economic reform in the constitutional level. "Any American efforts to preserve Yugoslavia would also put Washington on a collision course with Germany, when German leaders were enjoying their first taste of real political power since World War II. Moreover, US President George Bush had declared a special relationship with Germany, the kind America used to have with England. "The United States thought that Germany would have to be largely responsible for the incorporation of Eastern Europe and Central Europe into the West because Germany was -- had a national interest, it was its neighbour, its periphery, and it was financially the most powerful country in Europe and had the resources to do it. "In the post-Cold War period, Germany wanted once again - the evidence is very clear - to recolonize Yugoslavia, to recolonize the Balkans. The United States tied itself to German policy through its need of German power and influence in stabilising Eastern Europe, Western Europe, through the exercise of dominion via the European community, now the European Union, and potentially eventually in the former lands -- in the lands of the former Soviet Union. The problem was that there was one very important country standing in the way of this and that was Yugoslavia. "While citizens of Croatia were initially divided over whether to remain in Yugoslavia, the separatists were led by the most extreme elements, remnants of the pro-Nazi Ustashi. As the New York Times columnist A.M. Rosenthal would write: In World War II, Hitler had no executioners more willing, no ally more passionate than the fascists of Croatia. They are returning from 50 years ago from what should have been grave, the defeat of Nazi Germany. "Adolf Hitler considered Yugoslavia to be an artificial creation of the hated Versailles Treaty which ended World War I. To break it up, he set up a puppet state and enlarged Croatia, which also included Bosnia-Herzegovina. As its leader, he appointed the fanatical Croat Ustashi Ante Pavelic. Pavelic had helped plot the assassination of King Alexander, Yugoslavia's first constitutional monarch, in Marseille, France, in 1934. "And it was the Germans, the German Nazis who picked out this dreadful Ustashi leader who had made quite clear that he favoured Hitler's solution to be applied, which Hitler's final solution to the Jews he wanted to applied to the Serbs and he made no secret of it. "Simon Wiesenthal, who tracked Ustashi fugitives for decades along with other Nazi war criminals, told an interviewer: 'I must admit, I am obsessed by the criminal character of the independent state of Croatia. Even the Germans were appalled by the crimes committed in it.' "How many men, women, and children died there? Hitler's special envoy to the Balkans, Hermann Neubacher wrote: Leaders of the Ustashi boast that they have slaughtered 1 million Orthodox Serbs. On the basis of official German reports, I estimate the number to be three-quarters of a million. "Most of these Serbian civilians perished in the notorious Croatian death camp Jasenovac, which straddled the Sava River between Croatia and Bosnia. The extermination of Serbs, Jews, and gypsies in Sarajevo was the task of top Muslim leaders who, with few expectations, collaborated with Hitler and the Croatians. "There was in occupied Bosnian, also under German patronage, a strong Muslim wing which was very anti-Western. It was represented internationally by the mufti of Jerusalem. You heard of his viciously anti-Western views, and he was brought to Sarajevo and mobbed by enthusiastic crowds. "After the war ended, Croatia and Bosnia were never de-Nazified. Not only were there no apologies to the Serbs, Jews, and gypsies, but attitudes remained frozen under the surface of Tito's official policy of socialist fraternity amongst the peoples. "Following the death of Yugoslavia's long-time leader Tito in 1980, right-wing emigre organisations took out an advertisement on the opinion page of the New York Times, stating that Yugoslavia would not survive and offering a map which included all of Bosnia as part of Croatia. It was a map nearly identical to the Nazi-created independent state of Croatia. By 1990, as Communism was collapsing in Eastern Europe, Croatia separatists pinned their hopes on a former communist general named Franjo Tudjman, who had been jailed for excessive nationalism by Tito in the 1970s. "You know, I met him very soon after he came out of the communist jail, while Tito was still alive. He had then championed the racialist national -- form of nationalism. And when he came out of prison, instead of doing what you would think a dissident would do and say to hell with the communists, he said, oh, well, it was nothing do with the regime, it's those horrible Serbs who were repressing us and the Serbs are responsible for everything, and the Serbs are guilty, and the Serbs had done it all. "Tudjman received important help from outside of Croatia in his rise to power. "The German secret service was enormously active in Croatia and in all of Yugoslavia trying, in the 1980s, to build bridges between what were called the national communists, Stipe Mesic, Franjo Tudjman, in Yugoslavia, and the Ustasha revanchist organisations which lived in the diaspora of Croatia, that is to say, all of the people of weight and influence who had fled the former Nazi puppet state in 1945. "Tudjman found it useful to come to terms with them and because he was running on this xenophobic platform, there was really no difficulty about it. What was difficult was when he was trying to sell his cause in the West and he managed to partly because he had a very good lobby, very effective and much more effective than the Serbian lobby, and partly because he covered up his intentions. "Tudjman often embarrassed his most important supporters such as German Chancellor Helmut Kohl. For instance, Tudjman had written a book minimizing the crimes of the Ustasha and claiming that the Holocaust was greatly exaggerated. Thank god my wife is neither a Serb nor a Jew, he told one interviewer. For the national flag, Tudjman chose a replica of the chequerboard emblem that flew over the Croatian death camps of World War II, where Serbs, Jews and gypsies were exterminated. "Tudjman's anti-Semitic views were covered beneath rhetoric acceptable to the West. With the help of Ruder and Finn, a high-powered American public relations firm, the New York Times found space for General Tudjman's new and misleading image on its opinion page. In the article, Tudjman promised that there would be no purges against the Serbian population in Croatia if it separated from Yugoslavia. "Tudjman declared that Croatia was for the Croats, that was his slogan, a racialist slogan. Croatia for the Croats, with the implication people who weren't Croats, and there was a very substantial Serb and Yugoslav mixed variety, didn't feel that had any -- they were in fact second-class citizens and he recognised them as such. "A full six months before fighting broke out, Serbs were purged from positions in government, news organisations, and the police. Their homes were dynamited in cities such as Zagreb, Zadar, and Dubrovnik. For the first time since World War II, Serbs in eastern Croatia began to flee across the Danube river. "The Serbs working in Croatian cities were required to sign loyalty oaths. Those who did not sign were fired; those who did sign were fired later. Serb homes, apartments, and businesses were attacked. "[No interpretation]. "Any doubt that Tudjman himself issued orders for the expulsion of Serbs in Croatia was removed by Tomislav Mercep, a senior member of Tudjman's ruling party, the HDZ. Mercep would later be identified by Croatian police reports as one of two Croatian leaders who directed death squads that murdered hundreds of Serbian civilians in Eastern Slavonia, around Vukovar and Osijek, in the fall of 1991. He received little press coverage in the West but Mercep was in many ways the spark is that set the fire of war in Slovenia, a disputed region of Croatia where the Yugoslav war began. "Mercep's co-leader of the Croatian death squads was Branimir Glavas of Osijek. Unlike more discreet members of the ruling HDZ party, Glavas made no secret of his identification with the World War II Croatian Ustashi, as he welcomed returning Croatian prisoners of war. "While some French intellectuals were hailing Croatia as part of the new Europe, old and familiar forces were at work. Osijek became a magnet for neo-fascist groups fighting with Glavas. They included British skinheads, German and Austrian neo-fascists, and followers of the French extremist Jean-Marie Le Pen. "[No interpretation]. "The United States, which soon adopted Germany's approach to the Balkans, ignored recent history and offered a simple explanation for the fighting which broke out in the predominantly Serbian region of Croatia which was known as the Krajina. Assistant Secretary of State Richard Holbrooke, who spent the early years of the Yugoslav war as the American ambassador to Germany, represented what became the official American view. "The Serbs started this war, the Serbs are the original cause of the war. "Those who tried to prevent the war saw it differently. "The Serbs in -- in Croatia and indeed outside Croatia had a very vivid memory of what happened in 1941, 1942, when Hitler declared Croatia as an independent puppet state, if you like. And the horrors that went on there and the murders of the Serbs were still very -- I mean, a very large number of Serbs were murdered at that time. I mean, hundreds of thousands. And I think it was very understandable that when Croatia declared its independence and promulgated a new constitution without any safe-guard for the 600.000 Serbs who still lived in Croatia, that the -- the Serbs were very perturbed about this. "From the beginning, the Serbs were blamed and they were partly blamed out of ignorance because nobody bothered to look back at the history, to put it within its historical context, and to see why the Serbs who lived in Krajina and the Serbs who lived in the area of what's called Bosnia and Herzegovina, why because of their historical experiences were so hostile to being under Zagreb or under Muslim Sarajevo rule. "In World War II, Serbs offered the first serious resistance to Nazi Germany on the mainland of Europe. Later in the war, the Serbian royalists, sometimes known as the Chetniks, organised the largest rescue of downed American pilots behind enemy lines. But US relations with the Serbs deteriorated greatly by 1989, symbolised by the stormy relationship between Slobodan Milosevic, the new leader of Yugoslavia, and Warren Zimmermann, the new US ambassador to Yugoslavia. "I think Warren came out of Vienna from his last post as an ambassador dealing mainly with human rights and his first action as ambassador was to go to Kosovo and embrace the Kosovo separatist leaders. And this automatically offended the relatively new Serbian leadership under Slobodan Milosevic. "By the late 1980s, ethnic unrest in Kosovo had already set the stage for the breakup of Yugoslavia. For Serbs who first inhabited the area in the 7th century A.D., Kosovo was the cradle of their civilisation, their Jerusalem, and home to their most revered monasteries. "A bit of history, unfortunately, is required here. The Albanians pushed Serbs out in the 19th century. The Serbs starting pushing Albanians out around 1904. The Albanians surged back in World War II under Italian protection and pushed Serbs out. "When the war ended, however, Marsal Tito decided to keep the Serbian refugees from returning to their homes in Kosovo. As a result Serbs lost their majority in the province. "Tito is very guilty of that particular drama of Kosovo. He made it much harder to solve that, almost impossible. "To keep a restive Albanian population within the Yugoslav Federation, Tito's 1964 constitution gave Kosovo autonomy as a province of Serbia. However, the autonomy was badly abused by Tito's Albanian communist cadres who permitted a campaign of violence to drive out the remaining Serbian population. "Life was made extremely difficult for the Serb minority, and it was here that the Kosovars began to push to have a pure, all Albanian, meaning racially pure, Kosovo in the areas where there were very few Serbs anyhow, they were pushing them out, and the Serbs used the word that it was ethnic cleansing and that's what it was. "Homes of Serbs were appropriated by Albanians. Orthodox Christian cemeteries and monasteries were desecrated. By the late 1980s, the Serbian population of Kosovo had gone from 50 per cent at the start of World War II to just 10 per cent. "At this time, Slobodan Milosevic emerged as the voice of Serbian discontent over Kosovo. Seeking to consolidate his political base in his own republic, Milosevic also spoke for Serbian minorities living in Croatia and Bosnia who feared the emergence of hostile separatist regimes. A lifelong political opportunist, Milosevic was willing to provide limited military support to the Serbs of the Krajina as long as it suited his own agenda. The Serbian leader's manoeuvres, however, deepened the chaos that accompanied the breakup of Yugoslavia. "I think he is enormously to blame for his treatment of Western powers. From the beginning of 1991, he regarded them as the enemy and he would not talk to them. "While Serbia's president shunned meetings with the American ambassador, separatist leaders were receiving a sympathetic ear from Warren Zimmermann, the American ambassador and his boss, Assistant Secretary of State Lawrence Eagleburger, largely ignored the provocations of separatists in Slovenia and Croatia who were backed by Germany and focused solely on the Serbs. "The two of them adopted a stance that was, from day one, blaming the Serbs for just about everything. Serbs were the target of all of the actions of the United States of America from the beginning. "So did American news organisations whose foreign correspondents relied heavily on the US embassy for their reporting. Yet the obsessive focus of the press with Milosevic served to divert attention from the role of Western powers in making an avoidable war inevitable. While some Western leaders called Milosevic an architect of the conflict, the first shots of the war had been fired by armed separatists in Slovenia and Croatia, strongly supported by Germany. "In hope of heading off disaster, the European community organised a constitutional conference in 1991, led by respected British diplomat Lord Peter Carrington, to find a compromise between those who wanted to separate from Yugoslavia and those who wished to keep it together. The problem was that administrative borders or internal frontiers devised by Tito in 1943 left one-third of the Serbian population out of Serbia, mostly in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia. "These frontiers were drawn in a very secretive and very -- in my view, very irresponsible way by Tito's inner cabinet while the war was still going on and they were never subject to a public debate or discussion. They were never endorsed. "The idea of giving each republic substantial economic and political autonomy meant that each was a kind of hierarchy of the party, and then there was -- in order to keep the country together you had to balance these political leaders, and Tito was very skilful in playing one off against the other or in some cases of playing them against their population. It was the substitute for democracy in the way that we know it, but it was also considered by many of his supporters throughout the population as necessary because, to their view, democracy led to national or, as we call them, ethnic parties, and that would then breakup the country and lead to civil war again. "As Yugoslavia slid towards civil war in 1991, two referendums were held on the same day in Croatia. Croatians voted overwhelmingly to separate from Yugoslavia, whilst ethnic Serbs, particularly those from Krajina region, voted by a similar margin to remain within Yugoslavia. A compromise favoured by European community negotiators would have permitted Croatia to leave the Yugoslav federation but would have permitted the regions where Serbs formed the majority to remain in Yugoslavia or to gain substantial autonomy. Serbs who lived in an independent Croatia would be guaranteed full citizenship and human rights protections. "In the capital city of Zagreb, Croatian President Tudjman seemed reluctantly prepared to accept this compromise which would have prevented a major military conflict. Germany, however, announced they would recognise both Slovenia and Croatia within Tito's administrative borders before the end of 1991. There would be no compromise. "The Serbs were bitter that the first act of a newly united Germany would be to divide the Serbs of Yugoslavia into at least three separate countries. A crucial opportunity to divide Yugoslavia by peaceful means was now threatened by Germany's action. "It broke up because [indiscernible] because once you go, two out of the six republics declare independence, that those two had no further influence from constitutional [indiscernible]. You had to ask the other republics whether they wanted their independence, which meant you had to ask Bosnia, and it was perfectly plain that Bosnia -- that there was going to be a civil war in Bosnia if you did do that. "UN Secretary-General Perez de Cuellar sent a strong letter to German leaders, warning that recognition would be a disaster. Germany and Austria's own ambassadors in Belgrade privately warned against recognition of Croatia. "The Germans risked being isolated, but the pressure from the -- from Kohl's party and from the huge lobby of -- Croat lobby in the southern parts of Germany and Bavaria particularly, were such that it was difficult for Genscher to go on postponing the support. "By the time the war started, the German public had already been prepared by the repeated attacks on the Serbs in an influential German newspaper in Frankfurt. The strident commentary of Johann Georg Reissmueller, which favoured Croatia and reviled the Serbs, any Serbs, all Serbs, reminded Peter Hanke [phoen] of the way Nazi propaganda minister Joseph Goebbels once characterised the Jewish race. "It was the German press in a form par excellence of the right-wing of Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung and its journalists that fundamentally influenced German policy. "German support for Croatian separatists received an unusual tribute, a musical thank-you on Croatian state television. "Serbian television broadcast Croatia's musical thank-you interspersed with World War II footage of cheering Croatian crowds in Zagreb welcoming Hitler's troops. "All sides used propaganda, but Serbian propaganda was aimed at the Serbian population to bolster Milosevic's power base. By contrast, Croatian propaganda was designed to win international support. With the help of public relations firm Ruder and Finn, Croatia successfully used the media to manipulate a larger audience, particularly Germany and US, to gain support for its separatist agenda. This was particularly evident in the reporting of the war around the resort town of Dubrovnik, a favourite vacation spot for German tourists. "Working through its Washington PR firm, the Croatian government managed to convince much of the world that Dubrovnik was being destroyed by the Serbs in unprovoked attacks which lasted for months during the fall of 1991. "The public has been led to believe that the federal army attack on Dubrovnik was not precipitated by anything but sheer malice. However, on August 25th, 1991, Croatian forces attacked a base in the Bay of Kotor, around the Bay of Kotor, and they were repulsed with heavy losses. "Yugoslavia troops based in Montenegro then fought their way up the coast, confronting Croatian forces near Dubrovnik. "Targets outside the old city were hit consisting mostly of hotels which had been taken over as barracks and spotter points by Croatian forces who also put refugees in the lower storeys of their own barracks and spotter facilities. "It was obvious that the Croats were using the old town as a defensive wall. They were firing from behind hospitals. They had a mortar position next to our hotel. The final straw for me was when there was this incredible bombardment in our hotel basement. Bang bang bang bang bang. The worst we had ever heard. And I was furious. And every one else was panicking. And I said to the manager who was down there with us, I said: I wish you would tell that chap with the heavy machine-gun in the floor above to stop firing at the Serbs because they're going to fire back. "Contrary to news reports, there was little damage to the historic old city. "Yes, it has been reported some 15.000 shells rained on the old city of Dubrovnik. I counted 15 mortar hits on the main street. The Yugoslav federal army could have destroyed the old city of Dubrovnik in two hours. It is not destroyed. "Washington Post reporter Peter Maz [phoen], who visited the old city several months after the fighting stopped, found Dubrovnik in what he described as nearly pristine condition. "There are many people who go to these scenes of mayhem and adventure who don't know where they are, who don't know the languages, cannot really communicate with the people and who take press handouts from the local authorities. So there is certainly an orchestrated effort on the part of the Croatian and the Slovenian, Austrian and German media to portray the Serbs as a bunch of howling Byzantine, uncivilized barbarians. "The facts on the ground, however, mattered little after first impressions had been made. Rather than admit that they had made a mistake, influential columnists on both sides of the Atlantic continued to write that Dubrovnik had been destroyed. Public opinion was tilted against the Serbs and towards Croatia's political goal - recognition as an independent state. These impressions helped strengthen Germany's resolve to lead a reluctant European community to recognise the separatist republics and thereby dismantle Yugoslavia. "To overcome British opposition to recognising Croatia, German Prime Minister Helmut Kohl offered British leader John Major a deal which left Britain free to disregard or opt out of the social provisions of the 1991 treaty creating a unified Europe which was being hotly debated in the British Parliament. This helped John Major politically at home, but Bosnia would pay a high price. "The French, who needed German help to stabilise France's currency, also dropped their opposition to recognising the separatist republics. "The United States, the only power strong enough to oppose Germany, began to waiver. Deputy Secretary of State Lawrence Eagleburger, who had once served as US ambassador to Yugoslavia and spoke Serbo-Croat, knew well the dangers of a wider war if recognition were extended before a settlement had been reached between the different ethnic groups. "I think the major lesson here is when you get involved in something like this with a thousand years of history underlying it all, you need to understand that once the dam breaks, the viciousness can be pretty awful, on all sides. "In the end, here also, peace would be sacrificed for domestic politics. There was an American election coming up. "When we finally went ahead and recognised, one of the reasons we did so was because it had become a major domestic political issue for us here. We have particularly a large Croatian-American community and Mr. Bush lost most of them in the election that he lost because they were unhappy with our having delayed as long as we did in recognising Croatia. "While German actions were encouraged the armed secession of Slovenia and Croatia, it was US diplomacy, particularly through Ambassador Warren Zimmermann, which helped light the spark for a war in Bosnia-Herz" --

utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Mr. Hadzic not have the authority as president of the SBWS government to nominate or dismiss any minister. Rather, the president, the SBWS government, and its ministers were responsible to the Assembly that elected them. Your Honours will hear testimony from one of those ministers, Stevo Bogic, who will tell you that the so-called Serbian national security guarding in the government's premises in Erdut was not and never was subordinate to Mr. Hadzic. Your Honours will hear evidence that Mr. Hadzic's close relations with the Croatian government caused many locals and Yugoslav officials to distrust him. Indeed, even Arkan, whom the Prosecution has repeatedly attempted to show as associate of Mr. Hadzic, had his own ulterior motives to monitor Hadzic and possibly interfere with his interactions with Croatian authorities. The Defence will present the evidence, for instance, showing that Arkan sought to impose himself and the members of his unit on Mr. Hadzic as security details; Mr. Hadzic, however, kindly but persistently refused. The Defence will present evidence that until 25th of February, Mr. Hadzic was not superior to any part of the Serb forces listed in the paragraph 11 of the indictment. Our witnesses will show, as some Prosecution witnesses have implied that the notion that Mr. Hadzic could order JNA personnel, either from regular or reserve units, was laughable, if not unrealistic. Nor did his position afford him the authority to control the police or the TO units in the RSK, let alone in Serbia. Nor would his position afford him even the remotest authority to command volunteers, such as Serbian Volunteer Guard, from Serbian Radical Party, White Eagles, Dusan Silni, Skorpions, or the others. Defence will produce evidence on Mr. Hadzic's legal and de facto power regarding the armed forces of the RSK. Your Honours will hear that Mr. Hadzic had never been informed by the JNA or any other authority about the crimes allegedly committed by these units. In addition, neither Mr. Hadzic nor his government and judiciary was in charge to investigate and process the crimes committed in the area of responsibility of the JNA. In addition, the Defence will also present evidence demonstrating that Mr. Hadzic had no either legal or factual control over the detention and prison facilities as described in the paragraphs 40 to 41 of the indictment. He was not able to influence on the condition of the detention or prison facilities, either in Serbia or in SBWS and RSK. Mr. Hadzic did not participate in deportation or forcible removal of Croats and other non-Serbs as described in paragraphs 44 and 45 of the indictment. He was not aware of such policy being formulated or practiced by state organs of SBWS, RSK, Serbia, or Yugoslavia. As Your Honours will hear from Mr. Hadzic and witnesses who were in the RSK police and judicial organs, Mr. Hadzic forwarded all complaints from international representatives to the competent police or judicial organs of RSK and got assurance that it will be taken in the proper procedure. The Prosecution has attempted to argue that the government's efforts to respond to the massive influx of Serbian refugees from Western Slavonia by accommodating them in abandoned residences was part of an anti-Croat government policy. That argument is completely divorced from reality. What was the reality? Simply this: People were scared, villages had been attacked, rumours ran wild in the media and the towns, and they left. Your Honours have heard evidence from Prosecution witnesses who described their departures from their hometowns. Your Honours will hear evidence from Defence witnesses - like Amanda Celar - who also escaped in the night. This was happening to Croats and Serbs alike. The entire country was in upheaval and homes were abandoned. The newborn government, barely able to function as it was, now had to deal with a massive influx of people from other parts of Croatia into their jurisdiction. The only short-term solution that the government could offer these newly arrived refugees was what it had to offer: The houses left behind. This was not, nor was it intended to be, permanent. This was not, nor was it intended, to favour Serbs or any ethnicity. The government was dealing with the reality on the ground and in the front lines. None of this amounted to some broader plan to permanently remove non-Serbs from the region. Indeed, both Prosecution and Defence witnesses alike will tell you that the measure was not permanent. Many people ultimately returned to their homes after the war. Indeed, the houses that had been temporarily occupied were better maintained when their owners returned than those houses which were left abandoned. In other words, the government took the best, short-term option available to it to accommodate the displaced, and when it did -- sorry. And when it did so, the outcome was better than if they had done nothing at all. These refugees would ultimately be ordered by the JNA itself to leave those accommodations later. Your Honours, it concluded my opening statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Hadzic, you have the floor for your 84 bis statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to greet you and, first of all, to thank you for allowing me to address you. From the beginning of the trial, I have only been listening and I had no opportunity to comment or to say anything. I suppose you know that is not easy, especially when hearing things that are not consistent with either my memory or the truth. Of course, I will tell you all about it in my testimony that is to follow. There are two main reasons why I decided to use my right to address you personally. The first reason is very important to me and I will tell you about it immediately, whereas the second one, I will explain it later. It's not important. If the situation not so tragic, I would say it was ridiculous. First of all, I wish to express my regret for all the victims that suffered in this war. I don't wish and I don't have the right to single out anyone in particular because they're all just victims. There are victims on all sides to the conflict, and I regret them equally. I will explain why I think so. From my birth in 1958, I lived in the Pacetin village, the municipality of Vukovar. From September 1997 to date, I was unable to return there. The first written trace of my village dates back to the 13th century, more precisely 1275. From that date until now, it has been a village with an overwhelming Serb majority, over 50 per cent. Only in the last century, the municipality in which Pacetin lies changed names ten times, although the village remained in the same place geographically. In the beginning of the 20th century, it was part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, and towards the end of that century, as well as today, it was in Croatia. It had never been in Serbia although it should have been because it was populated by Serbs. In four different versions that state was called Yugoslavia. Many inhabitants of Pacetin lost their lives in the Second World War. Some were active fighters against fascism and some were civilian victims of fascist terror. Not then, in 1941, or later in 1991, nobody left to wage war from Pacetin. The war found us all in our homes. Due to the tragic experiences we had from the Second World War, nobody wished a new one, and of course neither did I. Not a single war has been our choice. But since I am on trial today, I will not say "our," I will say "my." I was no hero or volunteer. I never had the dilemma whether I should run away as a deserter. In keeping with my constitutional obligations, I remained there to defend the constitutional order of the only legal state that existed then, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I did everything I did as Goran Hadzic, son of Branko. I had no nickname or secret name. My motto was: Wars begin with negotiations and end in negotiations. It's better to negotiate for years than to wage war for one day. That is still my opinion today. I had the usual fear of war, like most people, but my fear was double because I had friends and family on both sides, especially since Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem is a relatively small area and we all know each other. In my fifth and sixth year of primary school, I ended up in the neighbouring Croatian village, Nustar. In the seventh year, I was in Borovo Naselje, which is a mixed population, whereas Nustar is a purely Croatian village. I finished high school in Vinkovci, a town with an overwhelming Croatian majority. Later, I studied at university in Osijek, which is a majority Croat town. I served my military service in Zagreb, and until 1991, I often travelled to Zagreb for different reasons. I was active in different sports. Mostly football and karate. I was a member of the stamp collecting society of Vukovar. I was employed in the company called Vupik in Vukovar. All these things I listed, my schooling, sports, stamp collecting, my job, everything was in the Republic of Croatia. I had many friends among all ethnic communities, but mostly Serbs and Croats. That is why my fear of war was at least double than the fears of those who were mobilised into a war a thousand kilometres away. In this war, I personally knew many of the participants on both sides. That's the reason why I never rejected any peace agreement. As one Prosecution witness, GH115, said, Your Excellencies, I was a positive exception among all Krajina politicians, a person who was prepared to talk even about the most sensitive subjects. Considering -- concerning my influence on military and political issues, I will testify in due course. Now I wish to emphasise that this influence was very small. I had almost none, despite my high political position. I read somewhere that one of the most important rules in history, when history covers an event, it has to take into account the time and the circumstances when the event happened. The same applies to the science of law. I am not a robot who could weigh every word he pronounces, nor am I a great mind or legal expert so as to be able to know at any given moment whether the information I have at my disposal is 100 per cent accurate, or whether my words could be misinterpreted before some court in the distant future. It must be taken into account, in particular, that I gave my statements during war events. I wish to emphasise that I never said or did anything with ill intent. I don't wish to defend myself here. I wish to testify, to help you gain a realistic picture of the events that unfolded in the 1990s. There is a question to which I cannot find an answer although I have been thinking about it for the past ten years. In the past 150 years, in every generation of my family there was only one male child. My great grandfather Ilija, my grandfather Sreto, my father Branko, myself, and my son, Srecko. In the Second World War, Ustashas slit the throat of my grandfather and set our house on fire. My father ran away to join the partisan troops when he was 18. The same army that killed my grandfather arrested my mother, who was then a teenager. She was not yet married to my father, and they took her to the Ustasha camp Tenje. That label was actually written on the camp. It's not my comment. It was called "Ustasha camp," that was the inscription on the gate. After the war, they moved her to Baden-Baden and later to Bielefeld, where the end of World War II found her. She returned home, walking along the railway lines from Vienna to Ljubljana. I was arrested and savagely beaten in 1971 by the regular police force of the Republic of Croatia. Most of these people are still employed in the same police force. That last event is a minor thing, of course, and I don't want to lend it any excessive importance because it's about myself, but I need it to raise a question to which there is no answer. What had my family done wrong to anybody, from 1943 to the 31st of March, 1991? How did we provoke this tragedy that befell us? Your Honours, could we, at this moment, please move briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have been charged with very serious crimes. It is for this Court to have the last say in this matter. I've already said that the first and real reason for addressing you is my wish to express my regret for all the victims. Now I want to say what the other reason is. If I were not in such a difficult situation, I could smile, like most of my friends, who followed the opening statement of the distinguished Prosecutor. He said, among the other sins attributed to me, that I destroyed mosques and churches. Of course, I did not destroy churches, and this Court is going to rule about that. But how could I destroy mosques when not a single one existed in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem or later on in the Republic of the Serb Krajina? I do not have the same kind of resources like the distinguished Prosecution, but as soon as I returned to the UNDU, I learned from the Croatian detainees how many mosques existed during the war in the Republic of Croatia and where there were. I found out that there was a mosque in Zagreb, that there was one in the village of Gunja, municipality of Zupanje, and that in Rijeka, a mosque was being constructed. It was only then that I really got scared and realised the extent of the problem I was facing. Is it possible that no one from this expensive and serious institution as the Office of the Prosecutor is could not have checked their assertions by making a single phone call? I was astounded I even thought that I was a victim of conspiracy. Now, if they did not check something that can be checked so easily, what else will I be up against? Then there was Witness GH169, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: (redacted). Then I realised that it was not a conspiracy at all or a conspiracy theory, that this was only natural, although it is not natural, that this is some kind of customary practice. As for all the things that were said against me, there is also this thesis that before my arrest, I was co-operative and reasonable, which is true. And after I was beaten up and tortured, I became an extremist. That is not correct. I can understand that everybody is applying their own logic, and how a particular person would behave in a similar situation, but that is not my line of thinking. I'm sure that this event in Plitvice was the result of a strange set of circumstances and that it was a tragic mistake. After leaving prison I did not change my political views. Everything was the same. Except for the fact that my health was impaired. I continued to communicate with the Croatian authorities as if nothing had happened. I communicated with Mr. Degoricija almost every day. In mid-April, as a matter of fact, I went to Zagreb to meet with Boljkovac, minister of police, and his assistant minister, Degoricija. After meeting with them in the MUP, I had a meeting with the republican prosecutor in Zrinjevac in Zagreb. Once the war started, it impossible to communicate any further. Your Honours, I'm an innocent victim and I fell victim by mistake. Why would I get any satisfaction for -- by taking revenge on innocent people just because they're not of the same ethnicity as I am? A few days getting out of Croatian prison, on 12th of April, 1991, I had a meeting at the American embassy in Belgrade. I was received by His Excellency Warren Zimmermann, together with Veljko Dzakula and Ilija Sasic. Ambassador Zimmermann clearly presented a position to us, a position of his government, inter alia, that they support a single Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and that they would not recognise or support the possible secession of any republic. My future conduct was based on this position presented by Mr. Zimmermann and I continued advocating the survival of the common state. In the beginning of autumn 1991, intensive contact started with the representatives of the European community and, after that, with the representatives of the United Nations. All of them - and I'm referring to these representatives - went to Belgrade first. They met with Serbian officials and the officials of the SFRY. After that, meetings were scheduled for me through the secretary of President Milosevic. These meetings were held in Belgrade, either in the Presidency of Serbia or in the residences of the government of Serbia. For example, as for meetings in The Hague and Paris, we went there on the plane of the government as agreed upon by Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Henry Wijnands. Perhaps the -- the meetings with representatives of the United Nations, Mr. Goulding and Mr. Cyrus Vance, are an even better example for this. I met with them in the Presidency of Serbia, in the same building where the office of Slobodan Milosevic was. The Vance Plan was signed by official Belgrade on our behalf. As for that plan, it directed us to Belgrade, because Serbia was supposed to be one of the guarantors of the implementation of this plan. This was a peace plan of the United Nations. The same organisation established a court and this court has indicted me for contacts with Belgrade, Slobodan Milosevic above all. And they are the ones who asked me to go and meet with Milosevic. I did not have any secret contacts. I did everything in public. As for all my meetings, both with the representatives of the international community and with the representatives of the federal state, the Republic of Serbia and the Autonomous Province of Vojvodina, I informed the members of the government about all of that regularly. I would like to take this special occasion that you have given to me to give a comment with regard to something that the distinguished Prosecutor said in response to the 98 bis submissions. Inter alia, he said that the fact that Goran Hadzic accepted the Vance Plan, and that is a peace plan, stands, but he says that this -- he did it out of his own interest. Every day through the media one can hear that certain states or certain peoples do something that is in their interest. The latest example are the developments in the Ukraine. Both parties there speak of their own interests, but there is a third party and a fourth party that has appeared there defending their own interests. Amazingly enough, there is even -- there are even threats to use weapons if all of that does not work. I don't think that is illegal. I'm not trying to say whether this is a good thing or a bad thing. Whereas it is held against me that I accepted this peace plan in my own interest. In whose interest was I supposed to accept this peace plan? I think that this kind of thinking would have surprised evening George Orwell if he were alive. Quod licet lovi, non licet bovi, a ox cannot do what Jupiter can do. I do not divide peoples and nations into oxen and gods. All are the same as far as I'm concerned. I'm grateful to them for having brought in GH28 as a witness, and through that person I found out that the state of which I'm a citizen established a military commission for co-operation with the Tribunal. Co-ordination, I'd like to point that out. I was shocked by this revelation. My citizen makes a distinction between it's important and unimportant citizens, first-class citizens, second-class citizens. An official commission is concealing evidence, co-ordinating false testimony, threatening witnesses and persuading them to give false testimony. In some previous proceedings and trials, the Prosecution called this its right name. In this case they behaved differently and they are supporting a thesis against which they were in the first place. We all had the opportunity of hearing part of the transcript from another case and the Prosecutor asked the Defence counsel whether he really believed that this government, meaning the government of the SAO Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem had any kind of influence. Clearly alluding to the belief of the Prosecution that the government did not have any power. Now this same institution is actually supporting the Defence from the Vukovar trial, as if this were a football game. So tactics are changed from one game to another. All the witnesses gave a solemn declaration stating that they would tell the truth and nothing but the truth. For the Prosecution it goes without saying that the truth is their only vehicle and that everything is being done in the interest of justice. There cannot be two truths with regard to the same thing that happened. Believe it or not, in the Dokmanovic case, the Prosecution had a third thesis as well. Or, rather, that was their first case and that was different from the other two cases. Different from this case, namely, and the Mrksic, Radic, Sljivancanin case. In some hypothetical situation, had I had the opportunity to influence military operations, there are three villages that are the very last anywhere in the world and those -- the very last ones that I would attack. That is Tordinci, Nustar, Marinci, my neighbouring villages. I'm sure that everyone who knows me at least a little bit knows why that is the case. Unfortunately, these villages suffered a great deal. According to the information that I have available, the only successful or the -- one of the most successful missions of the UN is the reintegration of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem into Croatia. This was carried out by Jacques Klein, an American general. Without any false modesty, I wish to point out that this success could not have been achieved and not to such an extent without the contribution made by my associates and myself. We established the civilian authorities and the police and we stayed with the people all the way up until 1996, as opposed to the well-known things that happened in the Western Krajinas. The people in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem had a choice to leave or to stay. Unfortunately, in other parts of Croatia, Serbs did not have that choice. They had to leave. As for what happened in 1991, all the way up until 1993, I was accused of all of that in 2003, 11 years after the Tribunal was established. I am a layperson, legally speaking, so I have no explanation. If all of that is correct, everything that the distinguished Prosecutor has said about me, how come it was made possible for me to live freely for 11 years? Is somebody supposed to be held accountable for that? Now there is another question. If the Prosecution needed 11 years to issue an indictment against me, how is it possible that I could have found out during two years of war about war crimes and how could I have organised prosecutions, and it is a well-known thing that I did not interfere in the work of the judiciary. If the allegations taped in the indictment are correct, that I ordered the destruction of Croatian towns and villages, expelled Croats from their homes, ordered and organised the killing of civilians and detainees, how is it possible that my parents stayed on in Croatia and lived in Croatia for nine years after reintegration, and my sister and children visited them every weekend regularly? And, finally, if anything is correct in this indictment against me, how is it possible, if my conscience is not clear, that my wife and daughter live in Croatia to this day. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, will you call your first witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Our first witness is Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hadzic, would you please take the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, could I ask you to state your name and date of birth for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Goran Hadzic. I was born on the 7th of September, 1958.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hadzic, as any witness, you are about to read the solemn declaration, by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I need to point out to you as well that the solemn declaration that you are about to make does expose you to the penalty of perjury, should you give misleading or untruthful evidence to this Tribunal. Could I ask you to read the solemn declaration now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Mr. Zivanovic, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hadzic, I'm not going to introduce myself to you, and you have already stated your name and surname and your date of birth. So my first question will be: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: I was born in Vinkovci in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you live after you were born?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: In the village of Pacetin, which is about 10 kilometres away from Vinkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
