utterances.text: Tell me, please, irrespective of the fact that you've already said that in your statement, something about your educational background.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: I attended grammar school in Vinkovci and I studied economics in Osijek. I did not graduate. I only graduated later in Novi Sad, not in Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you employed? If yes, where were you employed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: I started working in 1983 in Vupik in Vukovar, which is an agricultural company. I worked in my own village, Pacetin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Who did you live with in Pacetin?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: I lived in my parents' house. My father, my mother, and my sister lived there. Then I got married, and I had two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Before 1991, what was the ethnic structure of the population of Pacetin?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Pacetin was a Serbian village, which means there was a majority Serbian population. I had the opportunity to look at a census from 1990 which shows that 1100 people lived in Pacetin. There were 100 Orthodox Roma, and a thousand Orthodox Serbs, which means that the village was 100 per cent Serb. Later on, there were migrations of people. Some Croats came to work in Pacetin, so the ethnic composition changed a little but not by more than 5 or 6 per cent all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us something about the interethnic relations in Pacetin before the war, that is.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: In Pacetin, the relations were always the same, before the war and after the war. There were no conflicts based on ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us about your family's views or your parents' views and attitude towards various ethnicities. Can you describe the spirit in which you were brought up with regard to the attitude towards other ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: My parents were members of the League of Communists. My mother -- my father was an anti-fascist during the war which means that I was brought up in a Yugoslav spirit. As a child, I didn't even know whether somebody was a Croat, a Serb, or a Hungarian. It didn't matter to me. In my house I never heard a reference to ethnicity and they did not discuss the topic at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you did not hear anything of that kind, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I was not clear enough. I did not hear anything about ethnicity, about somebody being referred to as a Serb or a Hungarian or a Croat. There were no comments to that effect. I was brought up to consider every human being a human being, and that was the extent of it, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me when did you become aware of ethnic differences that existed either in Pacetin or in the general area?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Since I went to the elementary school in Pacetin for four years, Pacetin is a small village so the -- that there were no eight grades. Our school was a branch school of the larger school in Nustar which is a Croatian village. Before the age of 10 or 11 I did not have any information whatsoever that would make me think of ethnic differences. When I first arrived Nustar, I encountered some differences for the first time but that was because children in Nustar went to church and we didn't. Their parents were smarter, in a way, if I may put it that way. They were not communists and they brought up their children in a better way, in the way that I bring up my children now. They went to church. And that's when I noticed some differences between us, but I did not pay much attention to all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And later on, what happened?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: When I completed elementary school, I enrolled in grammar school in Vinkovci. Vinkovci had a Croatian majority. There were about 90 per cent Croats and about 10 per cent Serbs and that was also the ratio in the grammar school. By then I already became aware of ethnic differences but I did not have any problems with Croats or vice versa. I believe that I had more friends among Croats than among Serbs. I'm talking about my grammar school time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm now going to show you a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we have 1D443, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please look at the map. Can you see the village of Pacetin there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you mark it for us, please.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you also see Nustar in this map, the village of Nustar?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Can you scroll up a little, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you can't see it? And what about Borovo Naselje; can you see that? Or, rather, Vinkovci, not Borovo Naselje. Vinkovci.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: No, I can't see Vinkovci. If you can't see Nustar, you can't see Vinkovci because they're very close, the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And now Borovo Naselje; can you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Borovo Naselje is close to Vukovar. You actually can't see the word spelled out but the streets marked in yellow, all that is Borovo Naselje. For example, Trpinska Cesta.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you put a circle around all that. Put an A next to the village of Pacetin; and then when you make the second circle, can you put a letter B next to that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would tender this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D106, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to called up 1D442 now. [In English] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The village of Pacetin is already marked here with the letter A. Can you confirm, looking from this perspective, that this, indeed, is the village of Pacetin?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see Nustar here?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you mark ...

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And put a letter B next to that.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see Vinkovci on this map?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Again, the image should be scrolled up just a little because Vinkovci is south of Nustar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We don't have to do that.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: They are very close to each other. Vinkovci is only about 5 kilometres away from Nustar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would tender this document too, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would tender this document as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D107.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hadzic, while you resided in Pacetin, in addition to your regular work, did you have any hobbies? What were your pastimes, what did you do in your leisure time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Cynology was my great love. I trained dogs. I raised dogs. And also I played football in Pacetin. And then in the grammar school, I started training karate. I continued in Vukovar and in Osijek. And then I was a junior football coach for two years, and then for the next two years I was the coach for the first team, for the main team.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us whether you had any contacts with people of other ethnicities, Croats or other ethnic groups, as part of your pastime activities?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Approximately 50 per cent of my contacts were with Serbs and 50 per cent with Croats. When it comes to dog raising, most of my friends were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What was your relationship --

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: We were on friendly terms. I never had any conflicts with anybody. I've never had, up to this day, any conflict with anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, let me now ask you this: How long have you sported a beard? When did you start growing a beard?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: After the democratic changes I was a member of the SDP, which was Racan's party. In the second round of elections, when the HDZ won the elections, in protest I started -- I stopped shaving my beard. So that was in 1992 [as interpreted], in the month of May. But only in the summer of 1990 that beard became a visible feature on my face. Before that, it was not very prominent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have some photos of yours here. So could you tell us at least approximately when these photos date back to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, 1D397.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, we -- I'll repeat the question due to the transcript error.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please repeat the date and the year. Could you repeat the year. When did you start growing a beard?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: I started growing a beard on the 6th of May, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Look at the photo, please. Who are you with?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: My daughter and my son.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us at least approximately when was this photo taken?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: There's no date, but let me tell you when my children were born so we can draw our own conclusions. My daughter was born in 1983. And my son was born in 1987. I can see a candle. That was my son's first birthday, which means that this photo was taken on the 8th of October, 1988.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, shall we continue this after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, Your Honour. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, please continue. Oh, just one moment, Mr. Hadzic. There is a short oral ruling. On the 1st of July, the Defence filed a motion to amend its Rule 65 ter exhibit list with the addition of 214 documents. Of these, a total of 47 documents are intended for use with Mr. Hadzic during his testimony, and the Defence requests that these documents be dealt with on an expedited basis. The Prosecution responded in relation to these 47 documents via an e-mail on the 2nd of July and through oral submissions on the 3rd of July, today. These 47 documents include: Ten documents which were disclosed by the Prosecution to the Defence on the 2nd of June, 2014; 32 documents which were provided to the Defence by Serbia on 3 January 2014; and five documents which the Defence labels as "other relevant documents." The Chamber notes that as of the 2nd of July, 2014, an English translation was not available to the Chamber in e-court for 26 of these documents. After considering the submissions of the parties, the Chamber is satisfied that, taking into account the specific circumstances of this case, good cause has been shown for amending the Defence's exhibit list to include the ten documents disclosed by the Prosecution on the 2nd of June, 2014, for which an English translation has now been provided in e-court. The Chamber notes that the bulk of the 32 documents from Serbia are untranslated and the Prosecution objects to the addition of the others. The Chamber will consider the addition of these documents after all the translations have been provided and it has received a full response from the Prosecution. The Chamber considers that the Defence has not demonstrated due diligence in adding the five documents labelled as "other relevant documents" to its Rule 65 ter exhibit list. However, with the exception of 1D03571, the documents were originally disclosed by the Prosecution and therefore have been in its possession. The Chamber accordingly will allow the addition of 1D03567, 1D03568, 1D03610, and 1D03611 to the Defence's Rule 65 ter exhibit list in the interests of justice. The Chamber will issue a decision on the addition of 1D03571 in due course. Mr. Zivanovic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, I will tender the document 1D397.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D108, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see the document 1398 -- no, sorry, 398, 1D398.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you see the photo?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was that photo taken on the same occasion as the previous one?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. The occasion was the same, so the day was the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would tender this document too, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D109.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hadzic, in your binder, immediately at the beginning, there are two photos, 399 and 400. I'm going to show them to you, but before that, could you please tell me whether you possibly think that they should be shown to the public or are there any reasons for those photos not to be shown? Because I'm going to ask you about the names of the persons depicted.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: There's no reason not to show the photos.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see 1D399, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you perhaps remember when this photo was taken?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date. I believe that it was taken in 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's a wedding photo. Certain people got married. Could you please tell us their names.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: This is the wedding of my friend Zoran Ovsic from Dalj.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would tender this document too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Objection on relevancy grounds. Without more foundation, Mr. President, I don't know that this Mr. Ovsic bears any connection with the case. It's a wedding photo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Through these details we'll find the exact date of his marriage. It was only purpose why I put this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The previous photos with his one-year-old son were from -- from which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: For his first birthday. He answered this. As far as I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah, he answered, he answered the question, but I don't have it in mind. What was the date of the first anniversary of your son, Mr. Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 8 October 1988.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Okay. So this -- okay. Please continue, Mr. Zivanovic. The objection is overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, is it tendered?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah. I thought you were -- you were -- you're not going any further into this photograph and the exact date of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll not. I'll try to find the exact date of their marriage and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D110, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And please have a look at photos 1D400.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When was this photo taken; can you tell us, please?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Well, when I look at my daughter, I would say that it was taken sometime in 1986 or 1987, in the summer of that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you. [Interpretation] And now can you please look at 1D401. That's another photo.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when this photo was taken?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: I believe it was sometime in 1985.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hadzic, when you spoke about your hobbies and when you mentioned dog breeding and sports, tell me, have you ever had an interest in poetry?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you write poems?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you love to read poetry, attend recitals, readings of poetry?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that's different. I used to read poetry with my girlfriend but never with a male friend. Maybe I read poems to my girlfriend when I was in high school and I attended one reading of poetry with a friend of mine, Branko Kovacevic, but that was before the war. He was a writer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was he an author?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: He was a poet, amateur, and he published a collection of poems. The promotion was in Vukovar. The presentation of that book was in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, can you tell us when you became involved in politics?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Until the outbreak of the war, I was never seriously politically involved. All my activities were at the level of my village and my local commune. Not even at the municipal level in Vukovar. My first position was as president of the SDS in the municipality of Vukovar. That was the first relatively high position for me, and before that, I was a secretary of the youth organisation of the League of Communists in my village. I was a deputy in the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar. That was my first real political position, a deputy for the SDP party.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When did you become a member of the League of Communists?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: As soon as it was possible by the rules, when I turned 18. I was then in my third year of university [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was the platform of that party regarding the national issue in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: The position of that party was that all nationalities and nations, as has been stressed many times, were equal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What was the position of that party toward the preservation of Yugoslavia and the very existence of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Well, at that time, until Mr. Racan changed his position, there was no other option, except united Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zivanovic, I just want a question to clear something up. Line 14, page 63, is it correctly written: When the witness turned 18, he was in his third year of university?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat the question just in case. I asked you when you became a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: My answer was when it became technically possible, that is to say, when I turned 18 and I was in my third year of high school in Vinkovci. Third year of high school, not university.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did there come a time when that party changed its name?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: It renamed itself from the League of Communists of Croatia into the Party of Democratic Change, SDP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you remain in the party after it changed its name?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What was the ethnic structure, the ethnic composition, of that party?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: You mean in the whole of Croatia or in Vukovar municipality?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, you can tell us about the whole of Croatia and the municipality of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: At the level of Croatia, it was majority Croat, because Croats were in the majority; whereas in the municipality of Vukovar, I would say it was half/half. Perhaps there was a larger number of Serbs, not by much, but I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When the party changed its name, was it before the multi-party system was introduced or on the eve of multi-party elections?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Since I am testifying under oath, I must stress I'm not 100 per cent sure. I will tell you my opinion. I believe it was during the transformation, before the multi-party elections, when different parties were created in Croatia, including the HDZ, the Croatian Democratic Union. It became a little bit passe for the party to call itself League of Communists, so they changed their name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, in those multi-party elections, did you participate in any way?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I took part to the utmost of my ability. I invested all of my time and effort to help SDP win.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you remind us of the year.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: 1989/1990. In fact, it was early 1990 because the second round of elections was in May 1990, so the first round must have been six weeks earlier, April 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said it a moment ago but I will still repeat the question. Were you elected to some position in those multi-party elections?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: In my local commune, I was elected on the SDP ticket as deputy to the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And how did the party fare at the elections?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: At the republic level, it lost because most Croats voted for the Croatian Democratic Union; but in areas where Serbs were the majority, it won, as it did in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say you were elected to the Municipal Assembly in Vukovar, can you tell us whom did you represent there? Which parts of the municipality of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: I represented my village, Pacetin. It was they who elected me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Until what time did you remain a member of the SDP party?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Until June 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was there any event that made you leave the SDP?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: There were constitutional changes to the constitution of the Republic of Croatia and Vukovar was required to accept these changes. Together with some other deputies, I advocated a rejection of these constitutional amendments because the new constitution of Croatia envisaged an independent Croatia, separate from Yugoslavia. I did not have specific reasons to fear this option, but I felt it was not a good thing. So I addressed the Assembly and said that our mandate was to represent citizens of a united Yugoslavia and nobody had the right to interfere with that mandate. And a large part of the population of Vukovar voted for staying within Yugoslavia, so without changing their mandate, without a right from their -- without the acceptance of the citizens they couldn't do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please speak more slowly.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: It was resolved by a compromise. The municipality of Vukovar proposed amendments to the constitution, which were crucial, essential, but nobody paid attention. When the vote came, I was one of the few who voted against, and all the media reports said that Vukovar accepted the constitutional changes. Nobody mentioned that Vukovar actually voted for amendments to the new republic of Croatia constitution. And I continued advocating remaining in Yugoslavia, which we were all citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, alongside SDP, was there any other political party in Croatia that worked for Croatia to remain within Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: There was a small party that nurtured its own legacy of the so-called Socialist Alliance of Working People. There was a gentleman called Mazar who headed that party, but they had no serious political weight and they disappeared from the political arena very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When did you find out that there was a Serbian Democratic Party in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Now I know that it was established in February 1990, but I didn't find that out immediately. I learned perhaps in March or in April, from media reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What did you hear about the party? What did you learn about that party from media reports?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot tell you very precisely. You can tell from the name that it was a Serbian party, that it was from Knin, and we learned that it was in favour of a united SFRY, that is to say, for Croatia to remain within united Yugoslavia. That was roughly what I knew about them. But in my mind, that option was closer to the right, whereas I was closer to the centre or perhaps leaning a bit to the left; because the HDZ was extreme right, and the SDS was leaning to the left, and perhaps just because this "Serbian" in the name, it seemed to me that it was leaning to the left. But I knew that the extreme right in Croatia was represented by the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you talk about left and right, you mean political orientation.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm telling that is what I thought about the SDS at that time. All I knew, in fact, was that it was Serbian. And later on, I realised they were a centre party.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When was the first time you heard and learned more about what happened in the Second World War to your parents and other people? When did you get a more detailed explanation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: In my family home, there was no talk about it. It was just one -- once mentioned that our house was burned down during the war. That's because our father at some point wanted a bank loan to restore the house and when he was refused, he said: Our house was burned down in the war and we can't even get a bank loan for it. I learned mostly from other people, from general conversations. I didn't find anything out from my parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, was any distinction made - and what kind of distinction - between Croats on one hand and Ustashas on the other? Was there a distinction, how was the word "Ustasha" used, if at all, in your circle?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: It was -- those were two totally different things. Ustashas fought together with Hitler, and we, both Serbs and Croats, fought against them. And when I grew up and at our gatherings, there was talk about Ustasha emigres who must not return to Croatia, people who blew up cinemas and railway stations. In my mind, those were -- that was such a small fraction of the Croatian people, one in a few thousand. But then the political situation changed, and those people who supported these emigres started calling themselves Ustashas. But still, there were not a large number of them. That's what they called themselves. I repeat: They were not ashamed of it. They were even proud of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge -- we're actually talking precisely about that now, this very small group that called themselves Ustashas. To the best of your knowledge, what was their attitude towards the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I heard of that saying that the position of the Serbs -- of the Ustashas was that one-third of the Serbs should be killed, another third should be christened, and a third should be expelled. I heard that while I was still in politics. So they were intolerant of the Serbs to a maximum, and they were very, very strongly in favour of an independent Croatia. Perhaps that was their dominant characteristic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me generally what was the position of the Serbs in your own setting about this proclamation of Croatian independence and secession?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, we did not believe that this option would work because it wasn't the policy of the Croatian people. When we wondered about whether this option was at all possible, we were afraid of it. This happened at -- in the late 1980s. There were many people who were direct participants in what happened from 1941 to 1945 that were still around at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what it was that people were afraid of?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Well, when people would talk about the war, a war is a war. People don't have to be afraid of a war in every situation but they were afraid of these crimes that were committed. For instance, my father told me that during the Second World War, a group of Germans, company-strength, logistics, they lost their way and they were in Pacetin and they stayed there for about two months, and he said: Had things stayed that way throughout the war, nobody would have left. The Ustashas didn't dare enter Pacetin because the Germans were there and nothing ever happened, but then as soon as the Germans left, then the Ustashas came back and bad things happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have a special reason to be afraid from the proclamation of an independent Croatia, at that time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I did not believe that that could have been proclaimed, but I did have reasons. How could I stay in that state? I did not see my future there at all. I did not know that all of these things that have happened, entering the European Union, having democracy, et cetera, I had no way of knowing that that would happen, but it was very hard to understand what was going on. I was afraid and I think that my fear was justified. The people that we called Ustashas, while we were there, ten years before the war, they appeared in Croatia and they were the loudest at the rallies of certain Croatian parties. They said that they would make their objectives come true, and that was a very painful thing for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that that was very painful for you, you say "for us," that's what you said. Those are your words. Who do you mean by that, "us"?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: I meant Serbs primarily but also quite a few Croats who had these anti-fascist traditions, because my friends, other people I knew who were Croat, were strongly opposed to that policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, at the time of this election campaign, before the multi-party elections and generally at the time, what was the atmosphere like in Croatia in general? Or, rather, actually, what were interethnic relations like?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Well, then they started deteriorating. There was this euphoria of these pro-Croatian parties, there were several of them, but it was the HDZ that was dominant at the time. That's when these rallies started. And it wasn't only rallies for the sake of rallies. They even organised people who travelled to these rallies. There were columns of 100, 200 cars. They carried flags. They organised celebrations. Oxen were roasted, and all sorts of things were being said. I have to clear on this. I met some people later and some people I met here, they were not the same, not all of them were the same. There were some normal people, some good people, but what we heard was the worst kind of information that one could hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in greater detail what were some of the things that could be heard at such gatherings or in such situations which caused the most concern on your part and the people who were close to you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Well, the best-known slogan was: Croatia to Croats, also, there have been enough Serb officials in Croatia and the Croats were just working, which was not true. It wasn't only Serbs who were the directors or managers. Also they were saying that Serbs could only work with shovels, meaning that they would not be in managerial positions any longer. Also there were some messages that had to do with specific things related to liquidations, and we heard what was said by the TO and also arming Spegelj, et cetera, but all of this was before the arming.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the situation was in terms of protection, police protection, protection by those organs which are, in a way, duty-bound to protect the population from any kind of harassment?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: For example, in the municipality of Vukovar, in the police station, there were about 60 policemen, who were among the best in the former Yugoslavia, upholding law and order. There were no problems whatsoever. After these pro-Croatian parties won, then hundreds of people came there. They got jobs in the police. I heard 500, but a policeman who testified here said that there were 700 of them in Vukovar. I find that incredible but apparently it's true. These are people who were not professional policemen. They were of different backgrounds and quite a few of them criminal records too. They were immediately given automatic weapons. Up until 1990, actually, I had never seen a policeman with long-barrelled weapons. I always saw policemen in uniform with pistols only. And all of a sudden, they started moving about in camouflage uniforms and there were so many of them, and this caused a great deal of anxiety. And it wasn't only me, but many other people I talked to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, was there any physical threat to citizens of Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: There were a lot of such threats. I was president of the SDS for the municipality of Vukovar and people had no one to complain to and then they came to me and complained, and I couldn't really do anything. But I heard that Serb houses and businesses were destroyed, were -- had hand-grenades thrown on them. Many cars were destroyed. Also from cars they would attack these Serb businesses and homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you something. Do speak slowly when you answer. We have a bit of a problem with following all of this.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: This has not been finished in the translation. I said: Unfortunately, even from police cars, this kind of thing -- well, I perhaps do not see this translation. Maybe I'm right, maybe I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The pace is too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that has been left out, but the interpreters have told you just now that you do need to speak more slowly.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that in your capacity as president of the SDS of Vukovar that people turned to you, can you explain why they turned to you, why they turned to you as president of a branch of a political party?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: I can explain. It was because we, in Vukovar, within our political work in the municipality of Vukovar, we had inter-party meetings, so all the parties that had their own members in the Assembly of the municipalities met once a week and tried to resolve problems. It was actually the HDZ and the SDS that really handled all of this, Mr. Tomislav Mercep and I. People could follow this in the media. So then people came to me and they complained, and they asked me to exert my own influence at these meetings so that this kind of thing wouldn't happen to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did they ever tell you about asking the police for protection, the law enforcement?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Well, they went to the police but there were no results. And I went to the police at least once a week, and I complained because of these problems. As for these people that I talked to, I saw that they were honourable and that they were well-intentioned. However, most of these other policemen did this on their own. Because the people I talked to were pre-war policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us try to explain this a bit, this last sentence of yours. Actually, the last answer you provided. You said that you went to talk to the police, policemen, about once a week, and that most of these other policemen did that on their own. Can you explain this just a bit? Who was it that you contacted and who did things on their own?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, it's unclear the way I put it, yes. Although it was a bit unclear to me at the time too. I talked to official -- officials at the police station in Vukovar. Some of them had been newly appointed and others were from the old system. However, for the sake of the truth, I have to admit that these were not bad people, ill-intentioned, the people I talked to. So my conclusion was that they did not have any control over those people who were creating problems and that they were not in a position to solve these crimes. Because this was some kind of a secret policy, if you will, clandestine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me - can you tell us - when did you become a member of the SDS? When did you join the SDS?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I joined at the end of May 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: How did that happen?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Well, when the HDZ won, as I've already said, on the 6th of May, 1990, I, like most of my friends who were ethnic Serbs, realised that we had no one to represent us before the Croatian authorities and that the interests of the Serb people are not being put into the background but even further away than that. And then a friend gave me the programme of the Serb Democratic Party and I saw that there were some positions there that I agreed with. The main thing was that they were in favour of Yugoslavia and also the rights of the Serbs within Croatia because, at that time, within Croatia, Serbs did not have any rights whatsoever, in the sense in which minority peoples have in other states or as Serbs have in Croatia now although they are a minority. Perhaps it is important for me to point out now that I, as a Serb from Pacetin, I always felt that Croatia was my country. That is interesting and that is true. And it with pride that I felt that way. I mean, I have nothing against Croats. I still have many Croat friends, say, from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and now they have more of a right to Croatia than I do; whereas Croatia has been my homeland and the homeland of my family for over 300 years. Croatia used to be the homeland of both us and the Croats. When the conflict started, the Croats wore badges saying: "Croatia is my homeland." And a relative of mine made a similar badge but without Croatian symbols and said: "Croatia is my homeland too." And that was the truth. Now, unfortunately, Croatia is no longer my homeland.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you joined the Serb Democratic Party --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Zivanovic, excuse me. I would like to go back to the question of political parties. Witness, correct me if I'm wrong, in -- during the elections, if I understood you well, there were two principal, or two most powerful political parties that ran in Vukovar. There was the HDZ, the Croatian Democratic Union, and there was also the Serbian Democratic Party. If I understood you properly, the Croatian Democratic Union was in favour of the independence of Croatia, whereas the Serbian Democratic Party worked towards keeping Serbia and Croatia in the Yugoslav Federation. If I understood you properly, the Serbs who wanted to stay in an independent Croatia didn't have any other choice but to join and become members of the HDZ, which means the party which was known as the Croatian Democratic Union; whereas the Croats who wanted a Croatia as a member of the Federation of Yugoslavia did not have another choice but to join the Serbian Democratic Party. Did I understand you properly? Were there only two -- the two parties that I mentioned, or were there any other possibilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You didn't understand me properly, but it must be my mistake. Probably I didn't explain things too well. During the elections in Vukovar, there was no Serbian party because the Serbian party of Vukovar was established only after the elections. The main parties that ran in Vukovar was the Croatian Democratic Union - you understood that properly - and the SDP, the Party of Democratic Changes. It was the successor of the League of Communists of Croatia. It was also a Croatian party. Most of its members were Serbs but also Croats who were in favour of staying in Yugoslavia. When the Croatian constitution changed, most of our members, members of the SDP joined the HDZ and opted for an independent state of Croatia, which is why I felt cheated and betrayed and that's why we established the Municipal Board of the Serbian Democratic Party of Vukovar. When Croats were with us, we did not need a Serbian party. I personally would not have established it. There was no need for it. When it comes to the Serbian Democratic Party, it ran during the elections in Knin, in that part of Croatia, not in Eastern Slavonia. Have I been of any assistance? Did you understand me better now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Now it's clear. So the Serbian Democratic Party was born after the constitution was changed in Croatia, and actually made Croatia into an independent state. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not after. It was in parallel. After Croatian nationalists won the elections, there was a new constitution and that happened after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Oh. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to clarify things a little bit more, could you please tell us when was the Serbian Democratic Party established in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: It was in February 1990 in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And what about its board in Vukovar, when was that established?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: On the 10th of June, 1990, in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the municipality of Vukovar, did the Serbian Democratic Party run in the local elections in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: No, because it had not been established yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did that party participate in the republican election which covered the entire state of Croatia in 1990?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did, but only in the western part of Croatia around Knin. It did not participate in Vukovar, Osijek, or Vinkovci. It did not have its candidates. It did not participate in the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether the Serbian Democratic Party in Knin - the one that you have just mentioned - win a certain number of seats in the Croatian parliament?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did. I believe a total of five or perhaps six. I think it was five.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And in the municipal elections in Vukovar, which two parties were the main runners or competitors, as it were, in 1990?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: There was the HDZ, the Croatian Democratic Union, and the SDP, the Party of Democratic Changes, headed by Ivica Racan. The HDZ's leader was Franjo Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question. Can you just briefly tell us who Ivica Racan was?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Ivica Racan is a late Croatian politician. He headed the Croatian League of Communists at the moment when democratic changes in Croatia were taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was he also the president of the SDP, i.e., the Party for Democratic Changes?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Croatian League of Communists simply changed its name and became the SDP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether the SDS, the Serbian Democratic Party, established some other branches, save for the one in Vukovar? And I'm talking about Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem when I ask you this.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: It did establish branches in all the municipalities in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. In Osijek, Vinkovci, Beli Manastir, and obviously in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: How did it happen that you were later elected as the president of the branch office the SDS in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: It was quite unexpected. I had really worked hard, but at that time, my educational level was low, my employment record was not that impressive, so I didn't really believe that I would be elected by the people. However, as a result of all those activities and seriousness in my work, I was put forth as a candidate, and that's how things happened. We are in open session. I don't want to talk about my competitors who ran against me, and, in any case, that has nothing whatsoever to do with politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: While you were a deputy in the municipality of Vukovar, you had some meetings - you said it yourself - with the political representatives of the HDZ, and you mentioned Tomislav Mercep. Could you please tell us what the purpose of those meetings was? Why were they needed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: The main reason, the only reason, was to reduce tensions, to calm the situation down, because the situation was getting out of hand completely. Let me just explain for the Trial Chamber. It's very difficult to understand. Try to imagine a situation where villages are mixed and in many of those villages, half of the villagers are Serbs, the other half are Croats, and they hold opposing views. And then they go into the same bars and they start duelling verbally and all of a sudden all hell breaks loose. And it's all about ethnicity, about ethnic issues, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What was the result of those meetings between you, representatives of the SDS on the one hand, and the HDZ on the other?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: I must admit that at first I co-operated with Mercep quite well. However, later, as the tendency was more obvious and it became more and more clear that Croatia wanted to leave Yugoslavia, our friendship kind of broke. We could not speak at the same level when problems were compounded. And those meetings were also attended by representatives of the Croatian Assembly. One of them was Mr. Degoricija. He came to Vukovar often. He was the president of the parliamentary commission for co-operation with municipalities. I believe that that was his position in the Croatian parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm now going to show you a document that you may remember. It was shown already during the trial. It's P61.50. Do you remember this document?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you recognise your signature on this document?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise my signature and my handwriting. Everything that is handwritten was written by me. The document is in the Latin script, and my signature is in the Cyrillic script.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether you have seen the stamp before and the date? You can see the stamp at the bottom of the document, don't you? Do you remember who stamped the document? Did you go somewhere and hand the document to somebody?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. In our official capacity, we went to the municipality of Vukovar, which was still in the Republic of Croatia, and we handed the document over to the Croatian officials. This is an official Croatian stamp. Nothing irregular about that stamp at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read the date on the stamp, i.e., the date that you entered yourself?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: It's the same date, the 14th of August, 1990, and it is also on that same day that this document was received by the recipient.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And now can you please look at the top part of the document, where it says: "Narodne Novine," the "Official Gazette." At the very top of the page.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It says here "Official Gazette." I suppose that this was an Official Gazette of Croatia at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the date on the left-hand side of the document?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain the discrepancy, how come that a document which was handed on the 14 of August, 1990, and received on that same date actually came from the Official Gazette which was published on the 25th of June, 1990?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: It's really hard to explain. It's almost impossible. I suppose I don't have the right to say that here, but I really -- I don't have an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Before the trial, did you see this in the Official Gazette?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you saw it the first time when it was shown to you here in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Never before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And now could you please tell me, at the time when you were a deputy in the municipality of Vukovar, who was its president? Who had been elected as its president?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was Slavko Dokmanovic a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: No, he was not. Not at that time. He probably became a member in 1995, not earlier than that. But I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When he was elected as the president of the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar was Dokmanovic a member of any political party at all?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was a member of the same party as me, the SDP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I see, Your Honours, that we have just one minute left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: If this is an appropriate time, Mr. Zivanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hadzic, this is the end of today's hearing. You know that you're still under oath. You know that that means -- from experience here in the courtroom, you certainly know that that means that you cannot talk about your testimony to anybody, and we laid out the possibilities of having contact with your counsel in a decision that has been -- has been filed by now. So we will see you again tomorrow at 9.00. Thank you. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
